properties.context: Encompasses all classes of items intended or used for inflicting harm, defense, or combat applications, ranging from traditional melee tools to modern firearms and emerging technologies.
properties.edge_cases: Items used for sport, utility, or display can sometimes be considered 'tools' rather than weapons (e.g., kitchen knives). Local definitions and intent of use can cause classification ambiguity.
properties.examples: Historic swords, hunting rifles, pepper spray, modern assault rifles, improvised explosives.

properties.context: Any weapon that expels a projectile by the action of an explosive. Covered by federal, state, and local laws regulating manufacture, sales, possession, and use. Includes handguns, rifles, and shotguns commonly owned by civilians, as well as specialized or military variants.
properties.edge_cases: Some air guns or paintball markers can be confused with firearms but lack the combustion-based discharge. Black powder muzzleloaders may also be subject to different regulations depending on jurisdiction.
properties.examples: Typical examples: semi-automatic pistols, revolvers, bolt-action rifles, shotguns for hunting or home defense.

properties.context: Cartridges or shells fired from firearms, consisting of a projectile (bullet), propellant (gunpowder), primer, and casing. Regulations often address caliber, material (e.g., lead vs. non-lead), and specific types (armor-piercing).
properties.edge_cases: Less-lethal rounds (rubber bullets, bean bag rounds) may or may not be classified as ammunition depending on local laws. Reloading components (powder, primers) are also regulated.
properties.examples: 9mm pistol cartridges, 12-gauge shotgun shells, .223 Remington rifle rounds.

properties.context: Handheld weapons or tools featuring a sharpened edge or blade, traditionally used for cutting or thrusting. Regulations often focus on blade length, type of opening mechanism, or concealed carry.
properties.edge_cases: Some utility knives (like box cutters) can be misused as weapons. Historical or ceremonial swords may be exempt from certain restrictions if kept for display or cultural events.
properties.examples: Kitchen knives, folding pocket knives, combat daggers, fencing foils, samurai swords.

nodes.label: Non-lethal personal defense items (pepper spray, stun guns)

properties.context: Instruments designed to incapacitate or deter attackers without causing fatal injury under normal use. May use chemicals, electricity, or blunt impact to achieve defensive effect.
properties.edge_cases: Excessive force or misuse can still result in serious injury or death. Some states treat high-voltage Tasers or high-concentration pepper spray more restrictively.
properties.examples: Pepper spray canisters, personal stun guns, handheld Tasers, collapsible batons (where legal).

nodes.label: Heavy arms restricted to military/LE (machine guns, artillery)

properties.context: Advanced or high-capacity weapons typically reserved for military or law enforcement. Strict federal and sometimes international controls limit civilian ownership or trade.
properties.edge_cases: Demilitarized or deactivated items (e.g., inert artillery shells) can fall outside certain regulations if permanently disabled. Certain pre-1986 registered machine guns remain legal for civilian ownership under the NFA.
properties.examples: Full-automatic machine guns, grenade launchers, anti-aircraft cannons, large-caliber sniper rifles used by armed forces.

properties.context: Substances or devices capable of producing an explosive or incendiary effect. Strictly regulated at both federal and state levels due to public safety risks.
properties.edge_cases: Some ‘explosives’ (e.g., fireworks) are regulated as consumer items under certain thresholds. Homemade or improvised bombs are always illegal. Industrial explosives for mining or demolition require licensing.
properties.examples: TNT, dynamite, flash powder fireworks, shaped charges, grenades.

properties.context: Short-barreled firearms designed to be fired with one hand or two. Includes pistols, revolvers, and derivative forms.
properties.edge_cases: A large-framed revolver with a very short barrel might be considered an AOW (Any Other Weapon) under certain conditions in NFA contexts. The presence or absence of a stock changes classification.
properties.examples: Glock 19, Smith & Wesson revolvers, compact carry pistols.

properties.context: Handguns with an integrated chamber and barrel, typically fed by a detachable magazine. Modern pistols are often semi-automatic.
properties.edge_cases: Some older designs (single-shot or pepperbox pistols) can cause confusion. Pistol braces or attachments may reclassify them under certain regulations.
properties.examples: 1911-pattern .45 ACP pistols, modern 9mm polymer-frame pistols.

properties.context: Handguns featuring a rotating cylinder with multiple chambers. Typically simpler mechanically but slower to reload than pistols. Valued for reliability.
properties.edge_cases: Some rare ‘top-break’ or ‘folding trigger’ revolvers can be restricted if considered novelty or disguised weapons. Caliber and frame size vary widely.
properties.examples: Smith & Wesson .38 Special, Ruger GP100, Colt Python.

properties.context: Handguns capable of fully automatic or burst-fire operation. Often smaller versions of submachine guns, regulated under NFA if not law enforcement/military.
properties.edge_cases: A semi-automatic pistol modified with an auto sear is also classed as a machine pistol. These conversions are typically illegal without NFA compliance.
properties.examples: Glock 18 (factory full-auto Glock), select-fire variants of the CZ Scorpion pistol.

properties.context: Long guns featuring a rifled barrel for stabilizing projectiles. Designed to be fired from the shoulder, used for hunting, sport shooting, and military/law enforcement.
properties.edge_cases: Short-barreled rifles (SBR) require NFA registration if barrel length is under 16 inches. Pistol braces can blur definitions between rifle and pistol forms.
properties.examples: Hunting rifles, bolt-action sporting rifles, AR-15 platform rifles (in semi-auto form).

properties.context: Manually operated rifles where the user lifts and pulls back a bolt to eject the spent casing and load a new round. Known for reliability and accuracy.
properties.edge_cases: Straight-pull bolt designs can be confused with semi-autos by the untrained. Some vintage military bolt-actions may be considered collector’s items.
properties.examples: Remington 700, Mauser K98, Ruger American, Savage 110.

properties.context: Fires one round per trigger pull, automatically cycling the next round. Includes popular civilian sporting rifles and many modern designs.
properties.edge_cases: Modifications to increase rate of fire (bump stocks, forced reset triggers) may reclassify them. Certain semi-auto rifles are labeled 'assault weapons' under some state laws if they have specific features.
properties.examples: AR-15 pattern rifles, Ruger Mini-14, AK-47 style semi-auto clones.

properties.context: Military firearms capable of selective fire (semi-auto or full-auto), chambered in intermediate cartridges. True assault rifles fall under strict federal controls (NFA).
properties.edge_cases: The term 'assault rifle' is often conflated with semi-auto-only 'assault weapons' in civilian contexts, but under military definition, it requires select-fire capability.
properties.examples: M16, AK-47, G36 in their select-fire configurations for military use.

properties.context: Full-sized rifles firing cartridges like 7.62x51mm NATO. Typically used by military forces historically or as designated marksman rifles. Heavier recoil and longer range.
properties.edge_cases: Semi-auto battle rifles (like an M14 or FAL) can be restricted under some 'assault weapon' laws if certain features are present.
properties.examples: FN FAL, M14/M1A, H&K G3 in 7.62 NATO.

properties.context: Rifles with a barrel under 16 inches or overall length under 26 inches. Classified as NFA items requiring registration and a tax stamp in the U.S.
properties.edge_cases: AR pistols with braces can function similarly but remain pistols if they meet certain criteria. Installing a regular stock on a braced pistol can convert it into an SBR.
properties.examples: AR-15 with a 10.5-inch barrel and a standard stock (registered as SBR), chopped AK variants.

properties.context: Long guns designed to fire cartridges typically loaded with shot (pellets) or slugs. Used for hunting, sport, and home defense.
properties.edge_cases: Short-barreled shotguns (SBS) are NFA items. 'Firearms' like the Mossberg Shockwave (with certain length parameters) may not be legally defined as shotguns under federal law.
properties.examples: Pump-action 12-gauge, semi-auto duck-hunting shotguns, over-under sporting shotguns.

properties.context: User manually operates a sliding forend to eject spent shells and chamber fresh ones. Common for sporting, law enforcement, and home defense.
properties.edge_cases: Detachable magazine-fed pumps can be restricted under some state laws. Pistol-grip only models may affect classification.
properties.examples: Remington 870, Mossberg 500, Winchester SXP.

properties.context: Fire one shell per trigger pull, automatically cycling the next shell. Popular for faster follow-up shots in hunting or competition.
properties.edge_cases: Some states restrict semi-auto shotguns with certain features (folding stocks, large magazines). Specialized competition shotguns may have extended tubes exceeding typical capacity.
properties.examples: Benelli M4, Beretta 1301, Saiga-12.

properties.context: Shotguns modified to have a shortened barrel (under 18 inches) or overall length under 26 inches, regulated as NFA items in the U.S.
properties.edge_cases: Any unregistered or illegally modified short shotgun is contraband. Certain 'firearms' with short barrels but no stock (like the Mossberg Shockwave) are not legally 'shotguns' if they’ve never had a stock attached.
properties.examples: A 12-gauge with a barrel hacked down to 12 inches. Illegal contraband if not NFA-registered.

properties.context: Compact fully automatic or select-fire firearms firing pistol cartridges. Typically used by special forces, SWAT teams, or criminals when obtained illegally.
properties.edge_cases: Civilian ownership requires NFA registration (pre-1986 for new transferrable items). SBR status can overlap if a stock is attached.
properties.examples: MP5, Uzi, P90 (in full-auto configuration).

properties.context: Any firearm capable of continuous fire with one trigger pull. Civilian ownership in the U.S. is highly restricted by the NFA and 1986 Hughes Amendment.
properties.edge_cases: Certain conversion devices or sears turn a semi-auto into a machine gun under the law. Belt-fed rifles also qualify if fully automatic.
properties.examples: M240, M249 SAW, M2 Browning .50 cal heavy machine gun.

properties.context: Firearms made outside commercial manufacturing, often lacking official serial numbers or quality control. Can include simple handcrafted guns or advanced DIY projects.
properties.edge_cases: Legality varies if they meet federal and state definitions. '80% receivers' turned into functional guns must comply with marking requirements after 2022 ATF rule changes.
properties.examples: Homemade single-shot pipe guns, kit builds using 80% polymer receivers, handcrafted muzzleloaders.

properties.context: Privately made firearms without serial numbers, often assembled from partially finished frames or 3D-printed components. Historically not illegal for personal use (if legal to own) but subject to recent stricter rules.
properties.edge_cases: Transfers or sales of homemade firearms typically require serialization under new federal guidelines. Some states outright ban possession of unserialized guns.
properties.examples: Polymer80 Glock-style pistols, AR-15 lowers completed at home without serials prior to 2022 ATF updates.

properties.context: Guns fabricated (fully or partially) via additive manufacturing (3D printing). They can be polymer or metal. Often associated with 'undetectable firearm' concerns.
properties.edge_cases: Design files shared online can trigger ITAR/EAR export control. Fully plastic frames must incorporate enough metal to comply with the Undetectable Firearms Act.
properties.examples: The Liberator pistol (first fully 3D-printed gun), FGC-9 (DIY semiauto in 9mm).

properties.context: Extremely simple firearms typically fashioned from household materials (pipes, springs). Low reliability and safety; used illicitly where guns are restricted.
properties.edge_cases: Even crude zip guns are subject to firearm laws. If functional, it’s a regulated firearm; building or possessing them without compliance is illegal.
properties.examples: A piece of pipe and nail contraption firing .22 LR, homemade .410 shotgun using metal tubing.

properties.context: Non-serialized components or attachments that can modify or enhance the performance of a firearm. Some, like silencers or auto sears, are heavily regulated.
properties.edge_cases: A seemingly innocuous accessory (e.g., a 'solvent trap') may be classified as a suppressor part. High-capacity magazines and certain triggers fall under specific bans in some states.
properties.examples: Optics, grips, tactical lights, muzzle brakes, sling mounts, rails, stocks.

properties.context: Devices attached to or part of a firearm’s barrel that reduce sound and muzzle flash. Strictly regulated under the NFA in the U.S.
properties.edge_cases: Homemade suppressors, 'solvent traps,' or oil filter adapters can be considered unregistered silencers. Some countries treat silencers as normal accessories; in the U.S., they require a tax stamp.
properties.examples: Commercially made .30-cal suppressors, integrally suppressed barrels, custom 3D-printed silencers.

properties.context: Parts or attachments that increase a semiautomatic firearm’s rate of fire or convert it to full-auto. Considered machine guns under federal law if they enable continuous fire.
properties.edge_cases: Even possessing an auto sear (without a registered host) can be illegal. Bump stocks, forced reset triggers, and 'Glock switches' have faced bans and legal scrutiny.
properties.examples: Drop-in auto sears, bump stocks, binary triggers, forced-reset triggers.

properties.context: Small devices that replace or modify a pistol’s rear plate or internal components to enable full-auto fire. Classified as machine guns under U.S. law.
properties.edge_cases: Often 3D-printed or imported illicitly. Simply possessing an unregistered sear is a felony, even if not installed.
properties.examples: Glock auto sear plates sold online or distributed covertly, 3D-printed ‘switches.’

properties.context: Replacement stocks that harness recoil to 'bump' the firearm, effectively increasing the rate of fire close to full auto. Banned federally as of 2019 (pending litigation).
properties.edge_cases: Some earlier state laws preempted the federal ban. Possession after the ban’s effective date is generally illegal without specific exceptions. The classification remains under legal challenge in certain circuits.
properties.examples: Slide Fire Solutions bump stocks for AR-15 or AK platforms.

properties.context: Trigger systems that fire one round on pull and another on release. Not widely banned at the federal level but heavily restricted in some states.
properties.edge_cases: If misused or altered to function like full auto, it can be reclassified. Enforcement varies by jurisdiction due to legal gray areas.
properties.examples: Franklin Armory binary triggers for AR or AK rifles.

properties.context: Triggers that mechanically reset forward under recoil, allowing extremely rapid subsequent shots. ATF has taken the position that many forced-reset triggers are machine guns.
properties.edge_cases: Possessing or installing certain FRTs can lead to federal charges if the ATF deems them full-auto conversion devices.
properties.examples: Rare Breed Triggers’ FRT-15, Wide Open Trigger, etc.

properties.context: Magazines capable of holding more rounds than a standard or legally defined limit (often 10 rounds in restrictive states). Federal ban expired in 2004, but many states have their own limitations.
properties.edge_cases: Grandfathered magazines can be legal in some jurisdictions if owned before a cutoff date. Some states define anything above 10 or 15 rounds as 'large-capacity.'
properties.examples: 30-round AR-15 magazines, 50-round drum magazines, extended pistol mags.

properties.context: Small explosive or chemical-filled devices designed to be thrown or launched. Fragmentation, stun, and smoke grenades each have unique payloads.
properties.edge_cases: Live fragmentation grenades are strictly prohibited for civilians. Inert or training grenades can be mistaken for real ones, leading to legal issues.
properties.examples: M67 fragmentation grenade, flashbang (stun) grenades, smoke grenades for signaling.

properties.context: Grenades designed to disperse shrapnel upon detonation. Lethal within a specific radius. Strictly controlled as destructive devices under the NFA.
properties.edge_cases: Possession of even one live frag grenade is highly illegal without specialized destructive-device permits. Collectors may own inert or de-milled versions.
properties.examples: M67, RGD-5, F1 fragmentation grenades used by militaries worldwide.

properties.context: Non-lethal devices producing a bright flash and loud sound to temporarily disorient targets. Commonly used in SWAT or military raids.
properties.edge_cases: Can still cause injury if used improperly or in confined spaces. Some states restrict civilian possession. Pyrotechnic composition classifies them as explosive devices.
properties.examples: M84 flashbang, 'flash sound diversionary devices' used by law enforcement.

properties.context: Grenades emitting smoke for signaling or screening. Generally less restricted than fragmentation or stun grenades, but still often considered pyrotechnics or destructive devices if mil-spec.
properties.edge_cases: Commercially available smoke grenades for airsoft/paintball can be legal, while actual military-grade smoke grenades may be regulated as destructive devices.
properties.examples: M18 colored smoke grenades in green, red, yellow; commercial paintball smoke grenades.

properties.context: Devices intended to explode with destructive force, including improvised explosive devices (IEDs), vehicle-borne IEDs, or conventional bombs. Highly illegal outside military or demolition contexts.
properties.edge_cases: Some commercial explosives used in construction or mining must be properly licensed and stored. Any improvised device is almost universally illegal.
properties.examples: Homemade pipe bombs, car bombs, large fertilizer-based explosives.

properties.context: Homemade bombs crafted from various materials (chemicals, shrapnel) for illicit or terrorist activities. Extremely dangerous and unpredictable.
properties.edge_cases: Any distribution of instructions or components can be considered aiding in bomb-making. Federal and state laws impose harsh penalties for IED manufacture.
properties.examples: Pressure cooker bombs, hidden roadside devices, nail bombs.

properties.context: A type of IED made by filling a tightly sealed section of pipe with explosive material and a fuse or ignition device.
properties.edge_cases: Even possession of raw materials with intent can be prosecuted. Often used in criminal or terrorist acts; highly unstable.
properties.examples: Metal pipe filled with black powder or smokeless powder, sealed with end caps.

properties.context: Bombs placed or built into a vehicle, used as a mobile explosive delivery system. High destructive potential, widely seen in terror or insurgent attacks.
properties.edge_cases: Box trucks, sedans, or motorcycles can be turned into VBIEDs if packed with explosives. Detection is extremely difficult for law enforcement.
properties.examples: Oklahoma City truck bomb (1995), or typical car bombs used in conflict zones.

properties.context: Explosive devices worn or carried by an individual intending to detonate and kill themselves along with surrounding targets.
properties.edge_cases: Rare in domestic contexts but a known tactic in international terrorism. Federal law treats planning or attempting these as terrorism offenses.
properties.examples: Suicide vests, belts, or backpacks containing explosives and shrapnel.

properties.context: Explosive devices placed underground or hidden to detonate from pressure, tripwire, or remote trigger. Often used in warfare, heavily restricted internationally.
properties.edge_cases: Civilian ownership is almost never legal. Some inert training mines exist for demonstration or collector purposes only.
properties.examples: Landmines, claymore mines, directional fragmentation mines.

properties.context: Mines designed primarily to injure or kill people, often scattering fragments upon detonation. Prohibited by many international treaties.
properties.edge_cases: Even stockpiling for defensive purposes is highly illegal in most jurisdictions. Some militaries have leftover stockpiles, with global efforts for demining.
properties.examples: PMN, bounding ‘Bouncing Betty’ mines, claymore configured for antipersonnel use.

properties.context: Mines designed to disable or destroy heavy vehicles or tanks. Usually require significant pressure or a shaped charge to penetrate armor.
properties.edge_cases: Not typically triggered by foot soldiers but still dangerous. Civilian ownership is virtually non-existent and globally discouraged.
properties.examples: TM-46 Soviet antitank mine, M15 US mine.

properties.context: Broad category of edged tools or arms with a cutting edge, including knives, swords, axes, etc. Often regulated for carry or concealment rather than mere ownership.
properties.edge_cases: Some local laws ban carrying large fixed blades or certain automatic opening knives. Collectible or ceremonial swords can still face restrictions on public carry.
properties.examples: Hunting knives, machetes, decorative swords, tactical tomahawks.

properties.context: Handheld cutting tools with a metal blade, used for utility or as a weapon. Blade length and mechanism (fixed vs. folding) often matter legally.
properties.edge_cases: Large Bowie knives or ballistic knives can face extra restrictions. State laws vary widely on concealed carry and open carry.
properties.examples: Folding pocket knives, kitchen knives, hunting knives, multi-tools.

properties.context: Knives with a spring-loaded blade that opens automatically via a button or switch. Federal law restricts interstate commerce; states have additional regulations.
properties.edge_cases: Certain ‘assisted-openers’ or knives with partial spring assist may or may not be classified as switchblades depending on local definitions.
properties.examples: Classic Italian stiletto switchblades, OTF (out-the-front) automatic knives.

properties.context: Double-edged blades designed primarily for thrusting. Historically used in close combat or as concealed weapons.
properties.edge_cases: Some states ban double-edged knives or classify them as 'dirks' or 'daggers' with additional restrictions. Collectible medieval or fantasy daggers might be exempt from certain local laws if displayed.
properties.examples: Push daggers, stiletto daggers, Fairbairn-Sykes fighting knife.

properties.context: Long-bladed edged tools or weapons. Machetes are often used agriculturally, while swords are typically for ceremonial, decorative, or historical re-enactment. However, both can be misused as deadly weapons.
properties.edge_cases: Carrying a sword in public may face local restrictions. Some places treat machetes like long knives with no extra regulation unless concealed or brandished.
properties.examples: Katana, European longsword, machete for brush clearing or sugarcane harvesting.

properties.context: Bladed tools with a head affixed to a handle, used for chopping. Can be adapted as weapons. Tomahawks historically used by certain Native American tribes.
properties.edge_cases: If carried for self-defense, might be considered a weapon. Some modern 'tactical tomahawks' are designed specifically as combat tools.
properties.examples: Woodcutting axes, tactical tomahawks, throwing axes used in sports.

properties.context: Implements designed to incapacitate by blunt force trauma, lacking a cutting edge. Can range from simple clubs to complex maces.
properties.edge_cases: Sports equipment (e.g., baseball bats) can be misused. Some telescopic batons are restricted for civilian carry.
properties.examples: Baseball bats, batons, nightsticks, war hammers, crowbars (if used as a weapon).

properties.context: Short to mid-length blunt instruments used to strike. Common in sports or personal protection.
properties.edge_cases: A baseball bat in a car trunk can be normal sporting equipment—or considered a weapon if other context indicates intent.
properties.examples: Wooden baseball bats, nightsticks, improvised clubs from pipes or wooden rods.

properties.context: Typically used by law enforcement or security personnel, can be collapsible or solid. Some jurisdictions ban civilian possession of certain types (e.g., spring-loaded).
properties.edge_cases: Extendable batons are often restricted. A baton used as a medical device (e.g., cane) might be exempt in some contexts.
properties.examples: Police-issue expandable batons, friction-lock batons, fixed-length riot batons.

properties.context: Historic or modern replicas with a blunt or spiked head attached to a handle, designed for heavy impact against armored targets.
properties.edge_cases: Generally not common in modern self-defense. Collectors and re-enactors keep them for displays or medieval events.
properties.examples: Medieval flanged mace, spiked war hammer, modern ceremonial replicas.

properties.context: Metallic or composite devices worn around the knuckles to enhance punching force. Illegal or restricted in many areas due to high potential for injury.
properties.edge_cases: Plastic or polymer knuckles may or may not be explicitly named in statutes. Some states define them broadly to include any reinforcing ring over the knuckles.
properties.examples: Classic brass knuckle set, novelty knuckle keychains, spiked variations.

properties.context: Weapons relying on flexible components (chains, rope, wire). Often require skill to wield effectively and can be discreetly carried.
properties.edge_cases: Nunchaku laws vary widely. A simple rope or chain can be considered a weapon if used with intent.
properties.examples: Nunchucks, three-section staff, garrotes used for strangulation.

properties.context: Traditional Okinawan weapon made of two sticks connected by a chain or rope. Often restricted or banned in certain jurisdictions.
properties.edge_cases: Some states have relaxed older bans. Others still classify them as illegal to possess outside martial arts schools.
properties.examples: Wooden nunchaku for martial arts, foam-padded versions for training.

properties.context: A handheld ligature (wire, rope) used to strangle an opponent. Historically an assassination tool, now extremely restricted or outright illegal.
properties.edge_cases: Even simple wires or cords can be used as a garrote. Intent is key in legal classification.
properties.examples: Thin piano wire with handles, rope fashioned into a choking device.

properties.context: Devices using electrical discharge to incapacitate a target by muscle disruption or pain compliance. Often used by law enforcement or civilians for self-defense.
properties.edge_cases: High-voltage stun batons or contact prods may have special restrictions. Some states treat Tasers as firearms or require permits.
properties.examples: Handheld stun guns, cattle prods, stun batons.

properties.context: Handheld or projectile devices delivering an electrical shock to incapacitate. 'Taser' is a brand name using propelled probes.
properties.edge_cases: Civilian possession can be illegal in certain localities. Voltage and wattage thresholds sometimes define legality.
properties.examples: TASER Pulse, law enforcement X26, handheld stun devices with two prongs.

properties.context: Weapons relying on chemical agents to irritate or incapacitate targets. Often regulated for civilian use (maximum content, strength).
properties.edge_cases: Some pepper sprays exceed legal concentration or volume limits. Tear gas launchers can be heavily restricted.
properties.examples: OC spray, tear gas canisters, riot control irritants.

properties.context: Oleoresin capsicum formula causing intense burning of eyes and respiratory distress. Commonly allowed but with volume or percentage caps in some regions.
properties.edge_cases: Bear spray may have higher capsaicinoid content than typical personal defense spray. Mailing pepper spray can require special labeling.
properties.examples: Keychain pepper spray canisters, large canisters used by security personnel.

properties.context: Irritant aerosols used for crowd control or personal defense. Typically cause eye and respiratory pain, disorientation.
properties.edge_cases: Stricter than standard pepper spray in some jurisdictions. Mace brand once used CN gas; now mostly OC or CS blends.
properties.examples: Police tear gas canisters, personal CN/CS self-defense sprays.

properties.context: Rounds fired from specialized or standard firearms that deliver blunt force instead of penetration. Intended to minimize lethality.
properties.edge_cases: Close-range use can still be fatal. Bean bag rounds or rubber bullets can cause severe injury or death if misused.
properties.examples: 12-gauge bean bag shells, 37/40mm rubber baton rounds.

properties.context: Fabric pouches filled with lead shot or similar material, fired from a shotgun at low velocity. Designed to subdue suspects without lethal penetration.
properties.edge_cases: At very close range, can break bones or kill. Typically used by law enforcement with training protocols.
properties.examples: 12-gauge bean bag munitions used by riot police or SWAT units.

properties.context: Projectiles made of rubber or rubber-coated metal. Used for crowd control or riot dispersal. Less lethal than standard bullets but still pose serious harm risk.
properties.edge_cases: Untrained civilian use might cause severe injuries. Some authorities limit them to specialized riot control units only.
properties.examples: 40mm riot control rubber rounds, rubber 9mm or shotgun cartridges.

nodes.label: Gun Control Act of 1968 (18 U.S.C. §921 et seq.)
International Traffic in Arms Regulations (22 CFR 120-130)
Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. §2051 et seq.)
Federal Hazardous Substances Act (15 U.S.C. §1261 et seq.)
Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act
Lacey Act (re: illegal wildlife, plant trade)

properties.context: Novel or cutting-edge weapon technologies that do not fall neatly under traditional firearm or melee definitions. May leverage electronics, directed energy, or advanced propulsion.
properties.edge_cases: Classification often unclear due to evolving designs. Regulatory bodies may treat them as firearms, destructive devices, or create new categories as technology advances.
properties.examples: Smart Guns, railguns, directed-energy devices, drone-mounted weaponry.

properties.context: Firearms equipped with biometric or electronic authorization systems, allowing only approved users to fire. Proposed to reduce unauthorized use.
properties.edge_cases: Retrofit kits or partial electronic locks may not count as true 'smart guns.' Reliability concerns or hacking vulnerabilities raise safety/regulatory issues.
properties.examples: Armatix iP1 (RFID watch), Biofire fingerprint-handgun, LodeStar 9mm with PIN/fingerprint lock.

properties.context: Use electromagnetic force (coil or rail systems) to launch projectiles at high velocity without chemical propellants. Primarily experimental or military.
properties.edge_cases: ATF may not classify them as firearms if no explosive propellant is used, but lethal capability can still bring them under weapon statutes. High-power designs are rarely in civilian hands.
properties.examples: U.S. Navy railgun prototypes, Arcflash Labs coilgun, hobbyist coil-accelerators shooting metal slugs.

properties.context: Weapons emitting focused energy (lasers, microwaves) to disable or destroy targets without projectile munitions. Under development for military anti-drone and anti-missile roles.
properties.edge_cases: High-power industrial lasers can be misused as weapons. Blinding laser weapons banned by international law; domestic enforcement may treat them under destructive device or assault statutes.
properties.examples: Navy LaWS laser system, Active Denial System (heat ray), handheld laser dazzlers for crowd control.

properties.context: Systems mounted on unmanned vehicles or operated remotely. Used by military UAVs or ground robots. Civilian weaponized drones typically illegal.
properties.edge_cases: Non-lethal variants (tasers, pepper spray) could still violate FAA regs. Autonomous vs. remote control is a major regulatory focus.
properties.examples: Armed MQ-9 Reaper UAV, police bomb-disposal robot with shotgun, civilian drones illegally fitted with firearms.

properties.context: Devices using sound or microwave radiation to disperse or incapacitate targets with minimal lasting harm. Employed in riot control or crowd dispersal.
properties.edge_cases: Misuse can cause permanent damage (hearing loss, burns). Some 'acoustic' devices may be unregulated if sold as a 'sound deterrent' yet function as a weapon.
properties.examples: Long Range Acoustic Device (LRAD), Active Denial System ‘heat ray,’ handheld sonic blasters.

properties.description: Firearms subcategory includes handguns, rifles, shotguns, typical civilian guns.
Bullets, shells, and all firearm ammo, plus components like powder or primers.
Edged weapons: knives, swords, daggers, etc.
Pepper spray, stun guns, tasers, batons, etc.
Heavy arms (machine guns, suppressors, artillery, missiles, etc.)
Commercial explosives, bombs, grenades, fireworks, flamethrowers.

notes: Firearms exempt from CPSC oversight; must meet industry standards/ATF rules
Design safety (avoid accidental discharge, liability if defectively designed)
Serial number & manufacturer marking required (27 CFR 478.92)
Imported firearms must show country of origin
Export often governed by ITAR Category I (small arms)
Imports need ATF authorization (18 U.S.C. 922(a)(3)); sporting-use test
Trademarks/patents protect gun designs
Counterfeit parts lead to Customs seizures
FFLs maintain transaction records (18 U.S.C. 923(g))
Parts from embargoed countries prohibited
Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. 2778) & ITAR for exports
Lead ammo can contaminate environment; EPA RCRA applies to shooting range cleanup
18 U.S.C. 922(b)(1): 21+ for handguns, 18+ for rifles/shotguns from dealers
Background checks required for dealer sales (Brady Act)
FTC Act prohibits deceptive ads (15 U.S.C. §45)
Cannot market to minors; PLCAA immunity doesn't override marketing regs
Exempt from CPSC consumer regs; primarily industry-driven standards
ATF & DOT rules for explosive classification and safe primer sensitivity
16 CFR 1500.83(a)(6): must bear common name, warning like 'Keep out of reach of children', manufacturer info
